'''Lawrence S.B. Goldstein''' (born February 20, 1956, in [[Buffalo, New York]]) is a professor of cellular and molecular medicine at [[University of California, San Diego]] and investigator with the [[Howard Hughes Medical Institute]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2005/07/18/AR2005071801323.html|title=Stem Cell 'Alternatives' Fog the Debate|author=Paul Berg, George Q. Daley and Lawrence S.B. Goldstein|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|date=July 19, 2005|accessdate=March 7, 2010}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Lawrence Goldstein {{!}} UCSD Profiles |url=https://profiles.ucsd.edu/lawrence.goldstein |access-date=2026-03-26 |website=profiles.ucsd.edu}}</ref>  He receives grant funding from the [[NIH]], the Johns Hopkins ALS Center, the HighQ Foundation, and the [[California Institute for Regenerative Medicine]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Dr. Lawrence Goldstein Receives the Revelle Medal |url=https://moorescancercenter.ucsd.edu/_modules/homepage/lawrence-goldstein-revelle-medal.html |access-date=2026-03-26 |website=moorescancercenter.ucsd.edu}}</ref> In 2020 he was elected to the [[National Academy of Sciences]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://scripps.ucsd.edu/news/five-uc-san-diego-professors-elected-national-academy-sciences|title = Five UC San Diego Professors Elected to National Academy of Sciences| date=29 April 2020 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Lawrence S. Goldstein – NAS |url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/lawrence-s-goldstein-da4a1t/ |access-date=2026-03-26 |website=National Academy of Sciences |language=en-US}}</ref>

==Biography==
Dr. Goldstein received his B.A. degree in biology and genetics from [[UCSD]] in 1976 and his Ph.D. degree in genetics from the [[University of Washington, Seattle]] in 1980. He did postdoctoral research at the [[University of Colorado at Boulder]] from 1980 to 1983 and the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] in 1983/1984.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The ISSCR Announces Establishment of Lawrence Goldstein Science Policy Fellowship |url=https://www.isscr.org/isscr-news/the-isscr-announces-establishment-of-lawrence-goldstein-science-policy-fellowship |access-date=2026-03-26 |website=International Society for Stem Cell Research |language=en-US}}</ref> He was assistant, associate and full professor at [[Harvard University]] in the Department of Cellular and Developmental Biology from 1984 to 1993 and moved to [[UCSD]] and [[HHMI]] in 1993. His awards include a Senior Scholar Award from the Ellison Medical Foundation, an [[American Cancer Society]] Faculty Research Award, and the Loeb Chair in Natural Sciences when he was at Harvard University.<ref>{{Cite web |title=PNAS Member Editor Details |url=https://nrc88.nas.edu/pnas_search/memberDetails.aspx?ctID=20011518 |access-date=2026-03-26 |website=nrc88.nas.edu}}</ref>

His research is focused on understanding the molecular mechanisms of intracellular movement in neurons and the role of transport failures in neurodegenerative diseases.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Stokin |first1=Gorazd B. |last2=Lillo |first2=Concepción |last3=Falzone |first3=Tomás L. |last4=Brusch |first4=Richard G. |last5=Rockenstein |first5=Edward |last6=Mount |first6=Stephanie L. |last7=Raman |first7=Rema |last8=Davies |first8=Peter |last9=Masliah |first9=Eliezer |last10=Williams |first10=David S. |last11=Goldstein |first11=Lawrence S. B. |title=Axonopathy and Transport Deficits Early in the Pathogenesis of Alzheimer's Disease |journal=Science |date=2005 |volume=307 |issue=5713 |pages=1282–1288 |doi=10.1126/science.1105681 |pmid=15731448 |bibcode=2005Sci...307.1282S }}</ref> His lab provided the first molecular descriptions of [[kinesin]] structure and organization, and also discovered important links between transport processes and diseases such as [[Alzheimer's disease]]<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.accessmylibrary.com/premium/0286/0286-21612523.html |title=Stem Cells An Unlikely Therapy for Alzheimer's.|publisher=[[America's Intelligence Wire]] (AccessMyLibrary.com)|date=June 10, 2004|accessdate=March 7, 2010}}</ref> and [[Huntington's disease]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Brain Transportation System Defect Linked To Huntington's By UCSD Team |url=https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2003/09/030925064722.htm |access-date=2026-03-26 |website=ScienceDaily |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Her |first1=Lu-Shiun |last2=Goldstein |first2=Lawrence S. B. |date=2008-12-10 |title=Enhanced sensitivity of striatal neurons to axonal transport defects induced by mutant huntingtin |journal=The Journal of Neuroscience: The Official Journal of the Society for Neuroscience |volume=28 |issue=50 |pages=13662–13672 |doi=10.1523/JNEUROSCI.4144-08.2008 |issn=1529-2401 |pmc=6671757 |pmid=19074039}}</ref> Goldstein has also had an active role in National Science policy. He has served on many public science advisory committees, has written about, spoken about, and been interviewed on numerous occasions on science issues by print and broadcast media, and has testified on a number of occasions in the U.S. House of Representatives and the Senate about NIH funding and stem cell research. As a cofounder and consultant of the biotechnology company Cytokinetics, Inc. he has also had an active role in private industry. Goldstein has also served as elected secretary of the [[American Society for Cell Biology]] (ASCB).<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.highbeam.com/doc/1G1-89513343.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121103060853/http://www.highbeam.com/doc/1G1-89513343.html|url-status=usurped|archive-date=November 3, 2012|title=UC San Diego's Lawrence Goldstein Elected Secretary of American Society for Cell Biology|date=July 24, 2002|via=[[HighBeam Research]]|url-access=subscription|work=Ascribe Higher Education News Service|access-date=March 7, 2010}}</ref>
